hook_text: That faint band of light across a dark sky is not a cloud. It is hundreds of billions of suns, and you are looking at them from the inside.
clip_script: Get far from town lights on a winter night and you will see a faint, glowing band across the sky. The San of the Karoo said a girl threw ashes and embers up to light the way home. In 1610 Galileo pointed a telescope at it and saw that the glow is countless faint stars. It is our galaxy, the Milky Way: hundreds of billions of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. From above it would look like a giant pinwheel, a spiral about one hundred thousand light years across, but flatter than a dinner plate. We cannot see that shape, because we live inside the plate, about halfway out. Look along the plate and the stars pile up into a band. And the whole pinwheel turns. Right now the Sun is racing around the centre at two hundred and thirty kilometres a second. One lap takes two hundred and thirty million years.
visual_style: A whiteboard night sky with a band of stars, binoculars breaking it into dots, then a pull-back to a spiral pinwheel with a small arrow 'you are here', then a side view of a flat disc with an eye looking along it.
pacing: From a view everyone can see, to a scale that changes how they see it.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find out why the Milky Way looks like a band and not a spiral.
